pairs.rationale: The witness wording closely matches Deuteronomy's requirement for establishing a matter: at the mouth of two witnesses and at the mouth of three. Deuteronomy also rejects a single witness. The third proposed visit is a different statement and is not converted into a count of witnesses.

The warning of not sparing on a future visit corresponds to the purpose of writing while absent so that severity may be avoided when present. Both concern the anticipated visit, with building up as the stated aim; no severe action is reported as already accomplished.

The demand for proof of Christ speaking with power corresponds to the earlier account of proclamation demonstrated in Spirit and power rather than persuasive wisdom. The stated Christ and Spirit formulations remain distinct.

Both connect life with Christ to His victory over death. Romans says those who died with Christ will live with Him and that the risen Christ no longer dies; Corinthians contrasts crucifixion in weakness with life by God's power and applies weakness and power to the speakers.

Both direct self-examination. Corinthians' earlier instruction places examination before eating bread and drinking the cup; this instruction tests whether the recipients are in the faith and recognize Jesus Christ in them. The immediate purposes differ.

The writer hopes the recipients will know that the speakers do not fail the test, after asking the recipients to test themselves. The change from you to we and the hoped-for recognition are preserved rather than turning both statements into one group's uncertain result.

The prayer that the recipients do what is honorable even if the speakers appear to fail corresponds to joy when the recipients are strong and prayer for their restoration. Both put the community's good ahead of the speakers' favorable appearance.

The earlier rejection of cunning and tampering with God's word in favor of making truth known gives a concrete ministry counterpart to acting for the truth rather than against it. The statements relate conduct and truth without making every clause identical.

Both contrast we are weak with you are strong. The earlier statement appears among contrasts of apostolic humiliation and the recipients' status; here the speakers expressly rejoice and pray for restoration. The different rhetorical settings are retained.
Both explicitly say the Lord gave authority for building up and not pulling down. The earlier defense of that authority is here applied to writing while absent to avoid sharp treatment when present.

Both connect instructions for community conduct with the assurance that the God of peace will be with the recipients. Corinthians also names love and urges restoration, shared mind and peace; Philippians calls for practicing what was learned and received.
Both combine a holy-kiss greeting instruction with greetings from fellow believers. The source says all the saints and the target all the brothers, with the two greeting clauses in a different order.

Both include the Holy Spirit within a threefold formula. Corinthians names the Lord Jesus Christ, God and the Holy Spirit with grace, love and fellowship; Matthew names Father, Son and Holy Spirit in the baptismal commission. The named titles, actions and formulations are kept distinct.
